passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Cancelled Tour Leg

emails.subject: Booking NP-5518 — cancelled glacier leg
emails.body:
Dear North Pass,

I booked your seven-day Coastal & Glacier tour, booking NP-5518, at $2,380 per person for two people. The glacier walk on day five was cancelled and replaced with an afternoon at a visitor centre.

I understand weather cancellations. Your guide said conditions were unsafe and I do not question that for a second — I would rather be in a visitor centre than on unstable ice.

My issue is what happened next. We were told at breakfast that a refund "would be handled by head office", and when I asked how much, the guide said she did not know and that it was not her department. We then spent the remaining two days of an expensive holiday not knowing whether we were owed $50 or $500. That uncertainty spoiled the rest of the trip far more than the cancellation did.

I am not asking you to compensate me for the weather. I am asking why nobody could tell me a number, and what the number is.

Regards,
Rufaro Chikwanha

emails.subject: RE: Booking NP-5518 — cancelled glacier leg
emails.body:
Dear Mr Chikwanha,

Your complaint is about the silence, not the weather, and you are right that the silence was ours and avoidable.

The number is $164 per person, $328 total, refunded to your card within five business days. That is the glacier operator's fee plus the specialist guide surcharge for that day. The visitor centre entry cost us $11 per person, and we have not deducted it — you did not choose that substitution and should not pay for it.

On why nobody could tell you: the guide genuinely did not know, and that is a failure of ours rather than hers. Our guides carry no pricing breakdown, so when a leg is cancelled they can describe what is happening and not what it is worth. She answered honestly and unhelpfully because we gave her nothing better to say.

From next season every itinerary carries a per-leg value on the guide's copy, so a cancellation can be answered with a figure on the spot rather than a referral. It costs us nothing and it is the whole of your complaint.

One correction to something I suspect you were told. Weather cancellations on this tour are not rare — the glacier leg was cancelled on eleven days last season out of roughly ninety departures. We should say that at booking rather than let it read as bad luck, and from next season the itinerary will show it.

Regards,
Helena Vasquez
Customer Care Manager

passages.title: Where Tourist Spending Actually Goes
passages.content:
Destinations promote tourism on the strength of what visitors spend, and the figure is usually accurate. What it conceals is how much of that money remains in the place where it was spent, which is a different question and the one that determines whether tourism makes a community better off.

Economists call the gap leakage. A visitor who books an international chain hotel through an overseas platform, eats at an operator owned elsewhere and takes an excursion sold by a foreign tour company may spend a substantial sum without much of it staying local. In some economies, particularly small islands dependent on imported food and fuel, the majority of gross tourist expenditure leaves within months. The headline spend is real; the retained share is what a local economy actually receives.

The pattern is not uniform, and the differences are instructive. Independent travellers who book accommodation directly and eat where residents eat retain far more locally than package tourists, despite spending less overall in absolute terms. Cruise passengers spend least per head ashore and generate the highest costs in port infrastructure, waste handling and crowd management — which is why several ports that competed for cruise traffic have since introduced caps or levies.

Employment shows a similar divergence between the visible and the actual. Tourism creates jobs in large numbers, and those jobs are disproportionately seasonal, part-time and low-paid relative to the regional average. Senior and technical roles in international operations are frequently filled by staff brought in rather than hired locally. A region can therefore report significant tourism employment while local incomes barely move.

Housing is where the effect has become hardest to argue with. Where short-term letting is unrestricted, residential stock shifts to visitor use because the nightly return exceeds a long-term rent. That reduces the supply available to residents and raises rents, and the effect concentrates precisely in the central neighbourhoods that make a place attractive to visitors in the first place. Several cities now regulate this specifically, having concluded that the market outcome was displacing the population the tourism was ostensibly built around.

None of this argues against tourism. It argues that gross visitor spending is a poor measure of benefit, and that the policies which change the retained share — supporting local ownership, regulating short-term lets, managing cruise volume — matter more than the policies that raise visitor numbers.

passages.title: Should Cities Cap Short-Term Holiday Rentals?

viewpoints.name: Councillor Ingrid Haugen
viewpoints.text: We introduced a cap and I would defend it, with one honest caveat. Rents in the central district stopped rising faster than the city average, which was the goal. What I cannot tell you is how much of that was our cap, because two other things changed the same year, and anyone claiming a clean causal number is overselling. The strongest case is not the rent figure. It is that eleven hundred flats returned to long-term letting, and those are countable.

viewpoints.name: Tomasz Wieczorek, property owner
viewpoints.text: I let one flat, the one I lived in before I married, and the cap treats me identically to a company running forty. That is my objection and it is narrow — I am not arguing that forty-unit operators should be unregulated. Write the rule so it bites on scale rather than on activity. A threshold above which you are a business, with the obligations of one, would have achieved the housing outcome without catching people who let a single property for part of the year.

viewpoints.name: Dr Saoirse Mbeki, housing economist
viewpoints.text: Both sides cite studies that do not support what they claim. Short-term letting demonstrably raises rents in constrained central areas — that finding is robust and replicated. What is not established is that capping it lowers them again by a comparable amount, because the stock returning to the long-term market is small relative to total demand and the two effects are not symmetrical. Support the cap if you like; do not promise a rent reduction it has not been shown to deliver.

viewpoints.name: Bilal Zaman, hotel workers' union
viewpoints.text: The conversation is always housing and rarely labour, which suits everyone debating it. Short-term rentals shifted accommodation work out of a regulated sector with contracts and inspections into cleaning arranged privately, paid by the unit, with no sick pay and no recourse. Cap it or do not, but if the work simply moves rather than disappearing, we have improved a housing statistic and left the people doing the labour exactly where they were.
